 A former Goldman Sachs quant and two professors found a stock pattern that shows up at the same time every day for at least 40 trading days. Here's how it works. Look at a normal stock chart. Up, down, and to the human eye, pure noise. But hidden inside it are ebbs and flows that come back again and again if you dig through the data. That's what this team did. The quant is Stephen Heston, as in the Heston model, and the study ran in the Journal of Finance. They took every trade in over 1700 New York Stock Exchange stocks for five years, cut into half hours. Here's what they found. Say Apple beats Tesla between 1 and 130 today. Well, tomorrow, at the same time, Apple tends to beat Tesla again, and the day after that. And it isn't just those two. Rank all 1700 stocks every half hour, and today's top 10% tend to beat the bottom 10% at the same time tomorrow. And the next day, for at least 40 trading days. Two whole months, which is kind of crazy. Meanwhile, at any other time of day, it's the opposite, and a jump tends to fade. And it wasn't just Mondays or January or tiny stocks. It's strongest in the first half hour of the day and the last. So who's behind it? The authors think it's big players in the background who trade at the same time every day. Index funds want to match the closing price, so they trade near the close every day. Big funds slice huge orders into small pieces with trading programs that run on the same clock. In one study, 92.5% of big orders finish the same day. And money flowing into a fund keeps flowing for months, so tomorrow it buys again at the same time. Even busy managers trade at set hours between meetings. Same buyers, same time pushing on the price. So how would a quant use it? Buy yesterday's winner just before that half hour and short the loser, meaning bet it goes down. You collect the gap. On paper, across all those stocks, that gap averaged about 0.03%. That sounds small, but on a billion dollars, that's about 300,000. And for high-frequency firms that trade billions every day anyway, timing it right adds up fast. The market looks random, but people trading it aren't. This paper was 29 pages. This video was under three minutes. You're welcome.
